title: Two float keys whose exponents have a million digits are two keys or a limit error, in bounded time
notes: The input is a mapping with the explicit keys `1e` and a million sevens, `2e` and the same million sevens (explicit, because an implicit key is limited to 1,024 characters, section 7.4.2 / production 154), and the plain key `k`. Both keys match the Core float expression (section 10.2.1.4). They stand for 1 and 2 times ten to the power of a number with a million digits, two different values, so by the kit's rule for floats outside the range of a double (docs/edit-semantics.md, Refusals) they are two keys; a library that does not hold such a value may refuse the document with a `limit` error; it must not call them duplicates. What the case bounds is the cost of deciding that: comparing the two keys by exact value must not work through the exponent more than a constant number of times per key (parsing a million digits into a big integer digit by digit is quadratic work), and the cost of one comparison must stay far below the quadratic bound. The case is a patch with a small pointer because the kit has no value for such a float and a pointer cannot hold a million digits; the edit replaces `k` and nothing else. The tag `convention` marks the exact-value rule; the input is about 2 MB and built from the recipe in case.json (docs/case-format.md), hence `slow`.

provenance.reference: A key identity that parsed the exponent of every float key as a big number, so two keys with a million-digit exponent took tens of seconds.
